clinicalPearls: There is a complete horizontal gaze palsy to one side (the 'one') combined with an internuclear ophthalmoplegia on the other side (the 'half')
In practice the only preserved horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye, which often shows nystagmus
The lesion damages the ipsilateral paramedian pontine reticular formation or abducens nucleus together with the adjacent medial longitudinal fasciculus
The abducting eye may sit in exotropia in primary position, termed paralytic pontine exotropia
Vertical eye movements and convergence are typically spared because their pathways lie outside the affected pontine region
Common causes are pontine infarction, demyelination, and less often haemorrhage or tumour
The addition of a facial nerve palsy from involvement of the adjacent facial colliculus produces the 'eight-and-a-half syndrome'
reference.pathophysiology: A single paramedian pontine lesion damages the abducens nucleus or paramedian pontine reticular formation on one side, abolishing all conjugate horizontal gaze toward that side, and simultaneously involves the neighbouring medial longitudinal fasciculus, which produces an internuclear ophthalmoplegia affecting adduction of the ipsilateral eye on gaze to the opposite side. The combined result is that the affected eye cannot move horizontally at all, while the other eye can only abduct. Ischaemia is the leading cause in older patients and demyelination in younger patients, with haemorrhage and neoplasm accounting for a minority.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated horizontal gaze palsy without internuclear component
Combined multiple ocular motor nerve palsies from skull base disease
Thyroid eye disease with restrictive limitation
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the pons and brainstem to localise the lesion
MRI of the brain and cord for demyelinating disease
Vascular imaging and stroke workup in older patients
Cerebrospinal fluid examination for oligoclonal bands where relevant
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies to exclude myasthenia
Assessment for associated facial nerve involvement
redFlags: Acute presentation with additional brainstem signs indicating infarction or haemorrhage
Progressive course suggesting a pontine mass
Reduced consciousness or long-tract signs implying extensive brainstem damage
New facial weakness indicating spread to the facial colliculus
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause; ischaemic and demyelinating lesions often improve with partial recovery of horizontal movement over weeks to months, though a residual exotropia and diplopia may remain.
pitfalls: Misreading the preserved abduction as normal gaze and underestimating the deficit
Failing to recognise the combined gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia as a single localising lesion
Overlooking an accompanying facial palsy that broadens the localisation
Not imaging urgently when an acute vascular cause is likely
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
